title: Real Analysis I
subject: Mathematics

cards.prompt: State the interval equivalents of absolute-value bounds and the triangle and reverse-triangle inequalities.
cards.definition: For r>0, |x-a|<r is equivalent to a-r<x<a+r, while |x-a|>r means x<a-r or x>a+r. The triangle inequality is |x+y|≤|x|+|y|, and the reverse triangle inequality is ||x|-|y||≤|x-y|. Nonstrict versions use the corresponding nonstrict endpoints.
required_concepts: An absolute-value upper bound gives an intersection interval; a lower bound gives an outside union.
State triangle and reverse-triangle inequalities in the correct directions.
major_error_concepts: |x-a|>r means a-r<x<a+r, and |x+y|≥|x|+|y| always.

cards.prompt: State the algebraic laws for limits of two convergent real sequences, including the quotient restriction.
cards.definition: If real sequences a_n→a and b_n→b and c is constant, then a_n+b_n→a+b, c a_n→ca, a_n b_n→ab, and |a_n|→|a|. If b≠0, then b_n is eventually nonzero and a_n/b_n→a/b. Convergence supplies the boundedness needed for product estimates; b_n≠0 at every finite index alone does not replace b≠0.
required_concepts: State sum, scalar, product, and absolute-value limit laws.
The quotient law needs a nonzero limiting denominator.
The denominator is then nonzero on a sufficiently late tail.
major_error_concepts: Since b_n is nonzero for every n, the quotient law applies even when b_n→0.

cards.prompt: Define Archimedean property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that natural numbers are unbounded in the reals equivalently reciprocals eventually fall below every positive epsilon.
required_concepts: The theorem that natural numbers are unbounded in the reals equivalently reciprocals eventually fall below every positive epsilon.
major_error_concepts: Taking n equal to one over epsilon without integrality or strictness.

cards.prompt: Define Bolzano-Weierstrass for real sequences. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence proved by nested intervals or monotone subsequence selection.
required_concepts: The theorem that every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence proved by nested intervals or monotone subsequence selection.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the entire bounded sequence converges.

cards.term: Cauchy sequence criterion in the reals
cards.prompt: State the quantified Cauchy criterion for real sequences and distinguish it from vanishing successive increments.
cards.definition: A real sequence (a_n) is Cauchy if for every epsilon>0 there is N such that |a_m-a_n|<epsilon for all m,n≥N. A real sequence converges exactly when it is Cauchy; the reverse implication uses completeness of R. Requiring only |a_(n+1)-a_n|→0 is weaker and does not suffice.
required_concepts: Every tolerance has one tail index controlling every pair of tail terms.
Real convergence and the Cauchy condition are equivalent by completeness.
Small successive increments alone are insufficient.
major_error_concepts: A sequence is Cauchy whenever a_(n+1)-a_n tends to zero, even if distant tail terms remain far apart.

cards.prompt: Define Completeness axiom of the reals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The statement that every nonempty real set bounded above has a supremum in the reals and its dual infimum form.
required_concepts: The statement that every nonempty real set bounded above has a supremum in the reals and its dual infimum form.
major_error_concepts: Treating the rationals as complete.

cards.term: Density of rational and irrational numbers
cards.prompt: Define Density of rational and irrational numbers. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The existence of both a rational and irrational strictly between any two distinct reals.
required_concepts: The existence of both a rational and irrational strictly between any two distinct reals.
major_error_concepts: Inferring density from countability or uncountability alone.

cards.prompt: Define Least-upper-bound proof pattern. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The two-obligation proof that s is an upper bound and every smaller number fails to be one.
required_concepts: The two-obligation proof that s is an upper bound and every smaller number fails to be one.
major_error_concepts: Showing only that the proposed value bounds the set.

cards.prompt: What is Nested-interval completeness theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns a nested family of nonempty closed bounded intervals into a common point and supports existence and completeness arguments; losing closedness, boundedness, or the finite-intersection structure can empty the intersection.
required_concepts: It turns a nested family of nonempty closed bounded intervals into a common point and supports existence and completeness arguments
losing closedness, boundedness, or the finite-intersection structure can empty the intersection.
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem to open intervals.

cards.prompt: State Nested-interval completeness theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The conclusion that nested nonempty closed bounded real intervals have nonempty intersection with uniqueness when lengths tend to zero.
required_concepts: The conclusion that nested nonempty closed bounded real intervals have nonempty intersection with uniqueness when lengths tend to zero.
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem to open intervals.

cards.term: Order and squeeze limit theorem: role
cards.prompt: What is Order and squeeze limit theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers a common limit through eventual order bounds and provides a basic comparison tool for sequences and functions; bounds with different limits or inequalities that do not hold eventually are insufficient.
required_concepts: It transfers a common limit through eventual order bounds and provides a basic comparison tool for sequences and functions
bounds with different limits or inequalities that do not hold eventually are insufficient.
major_error_concepts: Using inequalities that hold only infinitely often.

cards.prompt: State Order and squeeze limit theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The preservation of eventual inequalities and convergence of a trapped sequence when lower and upper bounds share a limit.
required_concepts: The preservation of eventual inequalities and convergence of a trapped sequence when lower and upper bounds share a limit.
major_error_concepts: Using inequalities that hold only infinitely often.

cards.prompt: Define Ordered-field structure of the reals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The compatibility of addition multiplication and total order together with positive-cone rules used in inequality proofs.
required_concepts: The compatibility of addition multiplication and total order together with positive-cone rules used in inequality proofs.
major_error_concepts: Manipulating inequalities without tracking sign.

cards.prompt: Define Quantified real-sequence convergence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The statement that a_n tends to L when for every positive epsilon there exists N such that n at least N implies absolute a_n minus L below epsilon.
required_concepts: The statement that a_n tends to L when for every positive epsilon there exists N such that n at least N implies absolute a_n minus L below epsilon.
major_error_concepts: Choosing N after seeing n or testing only one index.

cards.prompt: Define Subsequence and inherited convergence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A sequence a_{n_k} with strictly increasing indices and the theorem that every subsequence of a convergent sequence shares its limit.
required_concepts: A sequence a_{n_k} with strictly increasing indices and the theorem that every subsequence of a convergent sequence shares its limit.
major_error_concepts: Allowing repeated or nonincreasing indices.

cards.prompt: Define Supremum and infimum. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The least upper and greatest lower bounds distinguished from maxima and minima that must belong to the set.
required_concepts: The least upper and greatest lower bounds distinguished from maxima and minima that must belong to the set.
major_error_concepts: Calling every supremum an attained value.

cards.term: Supremum proof idea for bounded monotone sequences
cards.prompt: Outline the supremum proof idea for convergence of a bounded monotone sequence.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** For an increasing bounded real sequence, completeness supplies the supremum of its range as the candidate limit, and the defining epsilon property of the supremum forces all sufficiently late terms into every epsilon-neighborhood of it. The infimum construction is the decreasing dual.
required_concepts: For an increasing bounded sequence, completeness supplies the supremum of the range as a candidate limit.
The defining epsilon property of the supremum makes all sufficiently late sequence values lie within epsilon of that supremum; the infimum argument is the decreasing dual.
major_error_concepts: Naming the supremum as the limit without using its least-upper-bound property to show that sequence values eventually enter every epsilon-neighborhood.

cards.prompt: Define limsup and liminf through tails and give their bounded-sequence interpretation.
cards.definition: For a real sequence, limsup a_n=lim_{N→∞} sup_{n≥N}a_n and liminf a_n=lim_{N→∞} inf_{n≥N}a_n, allowing extended-real values. Tail suprema decrease and tail infima increase. For a bounded sequence these are the largest and smallest subsequential limits, not necessarily values attained by any term. Convergence to a finite L is equivalent to both being L.
required_concepts: State the limits of tail supremum and tail infimum.
Allow extended-real values; bounded sequences have the subsequential-extrema interpretation.
They ignore finitely many early terms.
major_error_concepts: The limsup is the largest value a sequence has ever attained, including any exceptional first term.

cards.prompt: Define Uniqueness of a sequence limit. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that one real sequence cannot converge to two distinct real numbers proved by disjoint neighborhoods or the triangle inequality.
required_concepts: The theorem that one real sequence cannot converge to two distinct real numbers proved by disjoint neighborhoods or the triangle inequality.
major_error_concepts: Saying limits are obvious without using both quantified tails.

cards.prompt: Define Upper and lower bounds. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The quantified properties that one real number dominates or is dominated by every element of a set with emptiness and carrier explicit.
required_concepts: The quantified properties that one real number dominates or is dominated by every element of a set with emptiness and carrier explicit.
major_error_concepts: Checking only several elements.

cards.prompt: What is Absolute convergence theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It promotes convergence of the nonnegative absolute-value series to convergence of the original series and legitimizes Cauchy-tail control; the converse fails for conditionally convergent series.
required_concepts: It promotes convergence of the nonnegative absolute-value series to convergence of the original series and legitimizes Cauchy-tail control
the converse fails for conditionally convergent series.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the converse.

cards.prompt: State Absolute convergence theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The result that convergence of the absolute-value series forces convergence of the original series by the Cauchy criterion.
required_concepts: The result that convergence of the absolute-value series forces convergence of the original series by the Cauchy criterion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the converse.

cards.prompt: What is Alternating-series theorem and remainder used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It proves convergence and supplies a one-term remainder bound for alternating series with decreasing terms tending to zero; alternation alone or nonmonotone magnitudes do not provide the guarantee.
required_concepts: It proves convergence and supplies a one-term remainder bound for alternating series with decreasing terms tending to zero
alternation alone or nonmonotone magnitudes do not provide the guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Using the theorem when magnitudes are not eventually decreasing.

cards.prompt: State Alternating-series theorem and remainder, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The convergence of decreasing nonnegative terms tending to zero under alternating signs with error bounded by the first omitted term.
required_concepts: The convergence of decreasing nonnegative terms tending to zero under alternating signs with error bounded by the first omitted term.
major_error_concepts: Using the theorem when magnitudes are not eventually decreasing.

cards.prompt: State the Cauchy–Hadamard radius formula, including zero/infinity conventions and the boundary limitation.
cards.definition: For sum_{n=0}∞ a_n(x-c)^n, let L=limsup_{n→∞}|a_n|^(1/n). The radius is R=1/L, with R=∞ when L=0 and R=0 when L=∞. The series converges absolutely for |x-c|<R and diverges for |x-c|>R; boundary points need separate analysis.
required_concepts: Use the limsup of nth roots of coefficient magnitudes.
State the reciprocal conventions for zero and infinity.
Separate the interior/exterior conclusions from unresolved boundary points.
major_error_concepts: If the nth-root limsup is zero, the radius is zero and the series diverges everywhere except its center.

cards.prompt: Define the Cauchy product and state an absolute-convergence condition guaranteeing the product-of-sums identity.
cards.definition: For series sum_{n=0}∞ a_n and sum_{n=0}∞ b_n, their Cauchy product has coefficient c_n=sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_(n-k). If both original series converge absolutely, the product series converges absolutely and its sum is (sum a_n)(sum b_n). This is a sufficient condition, not a claim that both absolute-convergence assumptions are necessary.
required_concepts: State the finite convolution defining each product coefficient.
Both absolute convergences are one sufficient hypothesis.
Under those assumptions the product sum equals the product of sums.
major_error_concepts: The Cauchy product coefficient is a_n b_n, and convergence of both original series always suffices with no extra conditions.

cards.prompt: Outline the Cauchy-tail necessity proof idea and state its nonconverse.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** If a series has Cauchy partial sums, then each term is the difference of two adjacent partial sums and therefore tends to zero. Contrapositively, failure of the terms to tend to zero rules out convergence; the converse is false.
required_concepts: For partial sums s_n of a convergent series, the Cauchy-tail condition implies that a_n = s_n - s_(n-1) tends to zero.
Contrapositively, failure of a_n to tend to zero proves divergence, while a_n tending to zero is not sufficient for convergence.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the necessary condition and claiming that terms tending to zero make the series Cauchy or convergent.

cards.prompt: Define Conditional convergence under absolute-series failure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof-classification in which the partial sums converge while the corresponding absolute-value series diverges and unrestricted rearrangement stability is therefore unavailable.
required_concepts: The proof-classification in which the partial sums converge while the corresponding absolute-value series diverges
and unrestricted rearrangement stability is therefore unavailable.
major_error_concepts: Calling a signed series conditional without establishing both claims.

cards.prompt: Define Conditional rearrangement phenomenon. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction that rearrangements of a conditionally convergent real series can change the sum or diverge under governed selection.
required_concepts: The construction that rearrangements of a conditionally convergent real series can change the sum or diverge under governed selection.
major_error_concepts: Calling a permutation harmless because it uses the same terms.

cards.prompt: What is Limit-comparison theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers convergence or divergence between positive-term series whose term ratio approaches a finite positive constant; zero, infinity, or a missing ratio limit requires a different comparison.
required_concepts: It transfers convergence or divergence between positive-term series whose term ratio approaches a finite positive constant
zero, infinity, or a missing ratio limit requires a different comparison.
major_error_concepts: Using the theorem when the ratio limit is zero or infinite without the one-sided version.

cards.prompt: State the two-way limit-comparison theorem and explain why zero and infinity are excluded from that form.
cards.definition: For eventually positive sequences a_n,b_n, if lim a_n/b_n=L with 0<L<∞, then sum a_n converges if and only if sum b_n converges. The finite strictly positive limit permits eventual constant-factor bounds in both directions. A ratio limit of zero or infinity does not give this two-way conclusion without additional one-sided reasoning.
required_concepts: Both terms are eventually positive.
The ratio tends to a finite strictly positive L.
The series converge or diverge together under those assumptions.
major_error_concepts: A ratio limit of zero always implies the two positive series have identical convergence behavior.

cards.term: Local uniform convergence inside the radius
cards.prompt: Define Local uniform convergence inside the radius. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The uniform convergence of a power series on every closed subinterval strictly inside its radius obtained by geometric domination.
required_concepts: The uniform convergence of a power series on every closed subinterval strictly inside its radius obtained by geometric domination.
major_error_concepts: Claiming uniform convergence on the entire open interval from pointwise convergence.

cards.prompt: What is Positive-term comparison theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It orders tails of nonnegative series to transfer convergence downward and divergence upward; reversing either inequality direction gives no valid conclusion.
required_concepts: It orders tails of nonnegative series to transfer convergence downward and divergence upward
reversing either inequality direction gives no valid conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Using a convergent lower bound to prove convergence.

cards.prompt: State both valid directions of the comparison theorem for eventually nonnegative series.
cards.definition: If 0≤a_n≤b_n for every sufficiently large n, then convergence of sum b_n implies convergence of sum a_n, and divergence of sum a_n implies divergence of sum b_n. Convergence of the smaller series alone or divergence of the larger alone gives no conclusion about the other. Finite initial changes do not affect convergence.
required_concepts: Require eventual nonnegative order a_n≤b_n.
Convergence transfers downward and divergence upward.
Do not reverse either inference.
major_error_concepts: Because a convergent positive series is below another series, the larger series must converge too.

cards.prompt: Define Power-series operation preview. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem-directed interface that local uniform convergence supports termwise continuity integration and differentiation after their separate hypotheses are proved.
required_concepts: The theorem-directed interface that local uniform convergence supports termwise continuity integration
and differentiation after their separate hypotheses are proved.
major_error_concepts: Differentiating term by term solely from pointwise convergence.

cards.prompt: What is Ratio-test theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It uses asymptotic multiplicative decay to prove absolute convergence when the ratio limit is below one and divergence when above one; the boundary value one is inconclusive.
required_concepts: It uses asymptotic multiplicative decay to prove absolute convergence when the ratio limit is below one and divergence when above one
the boundary value one is inconclusive.
major_error_concepts: Applying the ratio test to a sequence with infinitely many zero terms without qualification.

cards.prompt: State the ratio-limit test for a series, including zero-denominator and threshold limitations.
cards.definition: Suppose a_n is eventually nonzero and L=lim_{n→∞}|a_(n+1)/a_n| exists, possibly infinite. If L<1, sum a_n converges absolutely; if L>1, its terms fail to tend to zero and the series diverges. L=1 is inconclusive. Infinitely many zero terms require a separately justified formulation rather than undefined division.
required_concepts: Ensure ratios are eventually defined and their limit exists.
L<1 gives absolute convergence; L>1 gives divergence.
L=1 is inconclusive.
major_error_concepts: A ratio limit equal to 1 proves divergence, and zero denominators can be ignored without changing the argument.

cards.prompt: Define Rearrangement of absolutely convergent series. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every permutation preserves the sum when the series is absolutely convergent.
required_concepts: The theorem that every permutation preserves the sum when the series is absolutely convergent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the same for conditional series.

cards.prompt: Outline the limsup proof idea for the root test, including why L = 1 is inconclusive.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** For L = limsup |a_n|^(1/n) below one, choose q strictly between L and one; eventual control by q gives |a_n| <= q^n and geometric comparison. For L above one, infinitely many nth roots exceed some q above one, so the terms do not tend to zero. The boundary L = 1 is inconclusive.
required_concepts: For L = limsup |a_n|^(1/n) < 1, choosing q with L < q < 1 gives eventual geometric domination |a_n| <= q^n and hence absolute convergence.
For L > 1, infinitely many nth roots exceed some q > 1, so the terms fail to tend to zero and the series diverges.
The limsup value L = 1 is inconclusive.
major_error_concepts: Treating an infinitely-often root bound as an eventual upper bound, or drawing a convergence or divergence conclusion when L = 1.

cards.term: Series as convergence of partial sums
cards.prompt: Define Series as convergence of partial sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The definition that sum a_n converges to S exactly when its finite partial-sum sequence converges to S.
required_concepts: The definition that sum a_n converges to S exactly when its finite partial-sum sequence converges to S.
major_error_concepts: Adding infinitely many terms as if ordinary associativity were automatic.

cards.prompt: Define Series Cauchy tail criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The condition that every sufficiently late finite block sum has small absolute value equivalent to convergence over the reals.
required_concepts: The condition that every sufficiently late finite block sum has small absolute value equivalent to convergence over the reals.
major_error_concepts: Checking only individual terms tend to zero.

cards.prompt: Define Closed set by open complement. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A subset whose complement is open with equivalent sequential-limit containment in metric spaces.
required_concepts: A subset whose complement is open with equivalent sequential-limit containment in metric spaces.
major_error_concepts: Extending finite union closure to arbitrary unions.

cards.term: Continuity by preimages of open sets
cards.prompt: Define Continuity by preimages of open sets. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The map property that every open target set has open preimage equivalent to epsilon-delta continuity in metric spaces.
required_concepts: The map property that every open target set has open preimage equivalent to epsilon-delta continuity in metric spaces.
major_error_concepts: Using images of open sets instead of preimages.

cards.prompt: Define Dense subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A subset whose closure is the full space equivalently every nonempty open ball meets it.
required_concepts: A subset whose closure is the full space equivalently every nonempty open ball meets it.
major_error_concepts: Equating dense with large cardinality.

cards.prompt: Define Diameter and bounded subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The supremum of pairwise distances and the existence of a finite-radius containing ball with equivalent finite-diameter behavior for nonempty sets.
required_concepts: The supremum of pairwise distances and the existence of a finite-radius containing ball with equivalent finite-diameter behavior for nonempty sets.
major_error_concepts: Calling boundedness compactness.

cards.prompt: Define Discrete metric topology. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric where distinct points have distance one making every subset open and every convergent sequence eventually constant.
required_concepts: The metric where distinct points have distance one making every subset open and every convergent sequence eventually constant.
major_error_concepts: Assuming boundedness yields a convergent subsequence.

cards.prompt: Define Distance to a subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: For a nonempty subset A of a metric space, d(x,A)=inf_{a in A}d(x,a). It is finite and 1-Lipschitz: |d(x,A)-d(y,A)|≤d(x,y). Moreover d(x,A)=0 exactly when x is in the closure of A. A nearest point need not exist. If A is empty, the extended-real convention inf empty=∞ is not a real-valued Lipschitz distance function.
required_concepts: Require A nonempty for the finite distance function.
State the infimum formula and 1-Lipschitz bound.
Zero distance characterizes closure, not necessarily membership or attainment.
major_error_concepts: Zero distance from x to A proves x belongs to A and is an attained nearest point even if A is not closed.

cards.prompt: Define Equivalent metrics by topology. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** two metrics generating the same open sets with stronger bi-Lipschitz equivalence distinguished from mere topological equivalence.
required_concepts: two metrics generating the same open sets with stronger bi-Lipschitz equivalence distinguished from mere topological equivalence.
major_error_concepts: Calling metrics equivalent because their formulas look similar.

cards.prompt: Define Homeomorphism and topological invariant. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A bijective continuous map with continuous inverse preserving open-set structure but not numerical distances.
required_concepts: A bijective continuous map with continuous inverse preserving open-set structure but not numerical distances.
major_error_concepts: Calling every continuous bijection a homeomorphism without compact-Hausdorff hypotheses.

cards.prompt: Define Interior closure and boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The largest open subset all adherent points and closure-minus-interior interface of a set under the specified metric.
required_concepts: The largest open subset all adherent points and closure-minus-interior interface of a set under the specified metric.
major_error_concepts: Using endpoint intuition for dense scattered sets.

cards.prompt: Define Limit point and isolated point. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction between every punctured neighborhood meeting a set and a point having a neighborhood containing no other set point.
required_concepts: The distinction between every punctured neighborhood meeting a set and a point having a neighborhood containing no other set point.
major_error_concepts: Requiring a limit point to belong to the set.

cards.prompt: State all metric axioms on a set X and distinguish the identity-of-indiscernibles condition.
cards.definition: A metric on a set X is a function d:X×X→[0,∞) such that d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y, d(x,y)=d(y,x), and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for every x,y,z in X. Nonnegativity is part of the codomain. Failure of the zero-if-and-only-if condition gives at most a pseudometric, not a metric.
required_concepts: Distances are nonnegative and vanish exactly for identical points.
Distance is symmetric.
The triangle inequality holds for every triple.
major_error_concepts: The function d(x,y)=0 for every pair on a two-point set is a metric because it is nonnegative, symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality.

cards.prompt: Define Open and closed balls. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric subsets defined by strict or nonstrict radius inequalities whose topological openness or closedness must be proved rather than inferred from names.
required_concepts: The metric subsets defined by strict or nonstrict radius inequalities whose topological openness or closedness must be proved rather than inferred from names.
major_error_concepts: Calling every closed ball compact.

cards.prompt: Define Open set by local balls. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A subset U where each point has a positive-radius ball contained in U with radius allowed to depend on the point.
required_concepts: A subset U where each point has a positive-radius ball contained in U with radius allowed to depend on the point.
major_error_concepts: Choosing one global radius for the entire set.

cards.prompt: Define Product metric construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A metric on a finite Cartesian product such as max or sum distance with coordinate convergence equivalence proved.
required_concepts: A metric on a finite Cartesian product such as max or sum distance with coordinate convergence equivalence proved.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all product metrics have identical numerical distances.

cards.prompt: Define Separable metric space. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A metric space with a countable dense subset and the proof consequences for countable bases at honors depth.
required_concepts: A metric space with a countable dense subset and the proof consequences for countable bases at honors depth.
major_error_concepts: Calling every metric space separable.

cards.prompt: Define Sequential characterization of closedness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space equivalence that a set is closed exactly when it contains limits of all convergent sequences from it.
required_concepts: The metric-space equivalence that a set is closed exactly when it contains limits of all convergent sequences from it.
major_error_concepts: Checking only one selected sequence.

cards.prompt: Define Sequential characterization of closure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space theorem that x lies in closure A exactly when a sequence from A converges to x.
required_concepts: The metric-space theorem that x lies in closure A exactly when a sequence from A converges to x.
major_error_concepts: Using the characterization unchanged in arbitrary non-first-countable topological spaces.

cards.prompt: Define Subspace metric and relative topology. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The restriction of a metric to a subset and the resulting open sets U intersect Y rather than ambient openness.
required_concepts: The restriction of a metric to a subset and the resulting open sets U intersect Y rather than ambient openness.
major_error_concepts: Calling relative openness ambient openness.

cards.prompt: What is Closed subset completeness theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It lets completeness pass from a metric space to every closed subspace and underlies fixed-point and compactness arguments on constrained domains; a nonclosed subset can contain Cauchy sequences whose limits escape.
required_concepts: It lets completeness pass from a metric space to every closed subspace and underlies fixed-point and compactness arguments on constrained domains
a nonclosed subset can contain Cauchy sequences whose limits escape.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every closed set is complete without complete ambient space.

cards.prompt: State Closed subset completeness theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The theorem that a closed subset of a complete metric space is complete and conversely a complete subspace is closed in the ambient complete or general metric setting with exact assumptions.
required_concepts: The theorem that a closed subset of a complete metric space is complete
and conversely a complete subspace is closed in the ambient complete or general metric setting with exact assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every closed set is complete without complete ambient space.

cards.term: Compact iff complete and totally bounded
cards.prompt: Define Compact iff complete and totally bounded. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space characterization joining Cauchy convergence and finite epsilon nets.
required_concepts: The metric-space characterization joining Cauchy convergence and finite epsilon nets.
major_error_concepts: Using completeness plus ordinary boundedness.

cards.prompt: What is Compact-image extremum-attainment theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It combines continuity with compactness to make image bounds attainable and supports global optimization on compact domains; boundedness of the image alone does not ensure attained extrema.
required_concepts: It combines continuity with compactness to make image bounds attainable and supports global optimization on compact domains
boundedness of the image alone does not ensure attained extrema.
major_error_concepts: Proving only boundedness and calling extrema attained.

cards.prompt: State Compact-image extremum-attainment theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The proof-level consequence that the real image of a nonempty compact domain under a continuous function is compact and therefore contains its supremum and infimum.
required_concepts: The proof-level consequence that the real image of a nonempty compact domain under a continuous function is compact
and therefore contains its supremum and infimum.
major_error_concepts: Proving only boundedness and calling extrema attained.

cards.prompt: Define Complete metric space. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A metric space in which every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
required_concepts: A metric space in which every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
major_error_concepts: Calling a space complete because every convergent sequence is Cauchy.

cards.prompt: Define Completion of a metric space. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A complete metric space containing an isometric dense copy of the original and unique up to an isometry fixing that copy.
required_concepts: A complete metric space containing an isometric dense copy of the original and unique up to an isometry fixing that copy.
major_error_concepts: Treating representative sequences as unique.

cards.term: Connected-image proof idea for intermediate values
cards.prompt: Outline the connected-image proof idea for the Intermediate Value Theorem.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** A continuous map sends a connected interval to a connected subset of the real line, and connected subsets of the real line are intervals. Therefore the image contains every value between its endpoint values, which recovers the imported intermediate-value conclusion.
required_concepts: A continuous image of a connected interval is connected.
Connected subsets of the real line are intervals, so the image contains every value between its endpoint values, recovering the imported Intermediate Value Theorem conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a continuous image has every intermediate value without establishing connectedness of the domain and the interval characterization of connected subsets of the real line.

cards.prompt: Define Connected metric subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A subset with no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open pieces and equivalent nonexistence of nontrivial clopen subsets.
required_concepts: A subset with no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open pieces and equivalent nonexistence of nontrivial clopen subsets.
major_error_concepts: Calling path connectedness and connectedness identical in every space.

cards.term: Connected subsets of the real line
cards.prompt: Define Connected subsets of the real line. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a real subset is connected exactly when it has the interval property between any two of its points.
required_concepts: The theorem that a real subset is connected exactly when it has the interval property between any two of its points.
major_error_concepts: Equating interval with open interval only.

cards.prompt: Define Continuous image of compactness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a continuous image of a compact set is compact by pulling an open cover back.
required_concepts: The theorem that a continuous image of a compact set is compact by pulling an open cover back.
major_error_concepts: Assuming inverse images require f to be invertible.

cards.prompt: Define Continuous image of connectedness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that continuous maps preserve connectedness and therefore real-valued images are intervals.
required_concepts: The theorem that continuous maps preserve connectedness and therefore real-valued images are intervals.
major_error_concepts: Using image preservation for discontinuous functions.

cards.term: Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space: role
cards.prompt: What is Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It equates compactness with closedness and boundedness in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, turning an open-cover property into a practical test; the equivalence does not extend unchanged to arbitrary metric or infinite-dimensional spaces.
required_concepts: It equates compactness with closedness and boundedness in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, turning an open-cover property into a practical test
the equivalence does not extend unchanged to arbitrary metric or infinite-dimensional spaces.
major_error_concepts: Applying closed-and-bounded compactness to arbitrary metric spaces.

cards.prompt: State Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The characterization that a subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact exactly when closed and bounded.
required_concepts: The characterization that a subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact exactly when closed and bounded.
major_error_concepts: Applying closed-and-bounded compactness to arbitrary metric spaces.

cards.prompt: Define Metric epsilon-delta continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The pointwise condition that for every target tolerance there is a source radius which may depend on the point and tolerance.
required_concepts: The pointwise condition that for every target tolerance there is a source radius which may depend on the point and tolerance.
major_error_concepts: Choosing delta dependent on the moving input point after quantification.

cards.prompt: Define Open-cover and sequential compactness equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space theorem joining the two compactness formulations through total boundedness or a Lebesgue-number argument.
required_concepts: The metric-space theorem joining the two compactness formulations through total boundedness or a Lebesgue-number argument.
major_error_concepts: Claiming equivalence in arbitrary topological spaces.

cards.prompt: Define Open-cover compactness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every open cover of a subset has a finite subcover with coverage relative to the ambient space declared.
required_concepts: The property that every open cover of a subset has a finite subcover with coverage relative to the ambient space declared.
major_error_concepts: Checking only one convenient cover.

cards.prompt: Define Sequential compactness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every sequence in a subset has a subsequence converging to a point of that subset.
required_concepts: The property that every sequence in a subset has a subsequence converging to a point of that subset.
major_error_concepts: Allowing the subsequence limit outside the subset.

cards.prompt: Define Sequential continuity equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space theorem that f is continuous at x exactly when x_n to x implies f(x_n) to f(x).
required_concepts: The metric-space theorem that f is continuous at x exactly when x_n to x implies f(x_n) to f(x).
major_error_concepts: Checking only sequences chosen conveniently for f.

cards.prompt: Define Total boundedness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that for every positive epsilon finitely many epsilon-balls cover the set which is stronger than boundedness in general.
required_concepts: The property that for every positive epsilon finitely many epsilon-balls cover the set which is stronger than boundedness in general.
major_error_concepts: Replacing epsilon-dependent finite nets with one bounded ball.

cards.prompt: Define Uniform continuity and Heine-Cantor. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The global epsilon-delta condition with one delta for all domain points and the theorem that continuity on a compact metric domain implies it.
required_concepts: The global epsilon-delta condition with one delta for all domain points and the theorem that continuity on a compact metric domain implies it.
major_error_concepts: Confusing continuity at every point with a uniform choice on a noncompact set.

cards.prompt: Define Convexity by secant slopes. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The inequality definition and monotone-slope characterization of a convex function on an interval independent of differentiability.
required_concepts: The inequality definition and monotone-slope characterization of a convex function on an interval independent of differentiability.
major_error_concepts: Using a graph picture without the quantified inequality.

cards.prompt: Define Convexity from derivative monotonicity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a differentiable function is convex exactly when its derivative is nondecreasing with supporting-line consequences.
required_concepts: The theorem that a differentiable function is convex exactly when its derivative is nondecreasing with supporting-line consequences.
major_error_concepts: Assuming f'' exists when only f' monotonicity is needed.

cards.prompt: Define Darboux property of derivatives. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every derivative has the intermediate-value property even when the derivative is discontinuous.
required_concepts: The theorem that every derivative has the intermediate-value property even when the derivative is discontinuous.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every derivative is continuous.

cards.prompt: Define Derivative algebra rules from limits. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sum product quotient and chain rules proved from difference quotients with all existence and nonzero conditions explicit.
required_concepts: The sum product quotient and chain rules proved from difference quotients with all existence and nonzero conditions explicit.
major_error_concepts: Using the desired product rule inside its own proof.

cards.prompt: Define Derivative as quantified linear rate. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The limit of the difference quotient at an accumulation point with domain-side and two-sided or one-sided convention explicit.
required_concepts: The limit of the difference quotient at an accumulation point with domain-side and two-sided or one-sided convention explicit.
major_error_concepts: Reading a tangent from a graph as proof.

cards.prompt: Define Derivative-sign proof of interval monotonicity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The mean-value argument that a nonnegative derivative on an interval implies nondecreasing behavior while an identically zero derivative implies constancy.
required_concepts: The mean-value argument that a nonnegative derivative on an interval implies nondecreasing behavior while an identically zero derivative implies constancy.
major_error_concepts: Inferring strictly increasing from a derivative that is merely nonnegative.

cards.term: Difference-quotient proof that differentiability forces continuity
cards.prompt: Define Difference-quotient proof that differentiability forces continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The quantified argument that a finite derivative at a point factors the function increment into a convergent hence bounded difference quotient and a vanishing input increment.
required_concepts: First material clause: The quantified argument that a finite derivative at a point factors the function increment
Remaining material clause: into a convergent hence bounded difference quotient and a vanishing input increment.
major_error_concepts: Assuming continuity implies differentiability or citing the implication without the factorization.

cards.term: Inverse derivative theorem in one variable: role
cards.prompt: What is Inverse derivative theorem in one variable used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers differentiability through a locally invertible one-variable map and computes the inverse derivative as a reciprocal; the original derivative must be nonzero and local invertibility must be established.
required_concepts: It transfers differentiability through a locally invertible one-variable map and computes the inverse derivative as a reciprocal
the original derivative must be nonzero and local invertibility must be established.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula where f' vanishes or f is not one-to-one.

cards.term: Inverse derivative theorem in one variable
cards.prompt: State a one-variable inverse derivative theorem with sufficient interval hypotheses and the correct evaluation points.
cards.definition: Let f be continuous and strictly monotone on an open interval I, differentiable at a in I, with f'(a)≠0. Its inverse is differentiable at b=f(a), and (f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(a)=1/f'(f^{-1}(b)). Strict monotonicity and continuity ensure an interval image and a continuous inverse; this does not justify reciprocation where f'=0.
required_concepts: Use an interval map with a continuous monotone inverse.
Require a nonzero derivative at the preimage a.
Evaluate the inverse derivative at f(a) and reciprocate f'(a).
major_error_concepts: At every b, (f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(b), regardless of whether b is the preimage point.

cards.prompt: Define Lipschitz bound from bounded derivative. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The mean-value consequence that the absolute derivative is at most M on an interval and therefore the absolute output difference is at most M times the absolute input difference.
required_concepts: The mean-value consequence that the absolute derivative is at most M on an interval
and therefore the absolute output difference is at most M times the absolute input difference.
major_error_concepts: Using the result across disconnected domains.

cards.prompt: Define Local extremum derivative condition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Fermat's theorem that an interior differentiable local extremum has derivative zero with endpoint and nondifferentiable exceptions preserved.
required_concepts: Fermat's theorem that an interior differentiable local extremum has derivative zero with endpoint and nondifferentiable exceptions preserved.
major_error_concepts: Claiming derivative zero implies a local extremum.

cards.term: Auxiliary-function proof idea for the Mean Value Theorem
cards.prompt: Outline the auxiliary-function proof idea for the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** Subtracting the endpoint secant line creates an auxiliary function with equal endpoint values. Rolle's theorem supplies an interior zero derivative for that function, which rearranges to the Mean Value Theorem conclusion.
required_concepts: Subtracting the endpoint secant line creates an auxiliary function with equal endpoint values.
Rolle's theorem supplies an interior zero derivative for the auxiliary function, which rearranges to the Mean Value Theorem conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Applying Rolle's theorem directly to the original function when its endpoint values differ, or omitting the continuity and differentiability hypotheses.

cards.term: Extrema proof idea for Rolle's theorem
cards.prompt: Outline the extrema proof idea for Rolle's theorem.
cards.definition: **Proof idea.** Continuity on the compact interval gives an attained extremum. If the equal-endpoint function is nonconstant, an attained maximum or minimum lies in the interior, where differentiability forces derivative zero; the constant case is immediate.
required_concepts: Continuity on a compact interval gives an attained extremum.
If equal endpoint values do not make the function constant, one attained extremum is interior, where differentiability forces derivative zero; the constant case is immediate.
major_error_concepts: Claiming equal endpoint values alone place a maximum or minimum in the interior without separating the constant and nonconstant cases.

cards.prompt: Define Second-derivative convexity criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sufficient and under appropriate regularity equivalent condition f'' nonnegative for convexity.
required_concepts: The sufficient and under appropriate regularity equivalent condition f'' nonnegative for convexity.
major_error_concepts: Calling isolated positive second derivative global convexity.

cards.prompt: Give a smooth nonanalytic counterexample and explain exactly why its Taylor series fails to recover it.
cards.definition: Define f(0)=0 and f(x)=exp(-1/x²) for x≠0. This function is C∞ on R and every derivative at 0 is zero, so its Taylor series there is identically zero. Yet f(x)>0 for every x≠0, so that series fails to equal f on any neighborhood of 0. Thus smoothness does not imply analyticity.
required_concepts: Give an explicit function and justify smoothness on a neighborhood of the expansion point.
Identify its Taylor series and establish that the function differs from that series arbitrarily near the point.
Conclude C∞ does not imply analyticity; zero Taylor coefficients are only one possible construction.
accepted_variants: Let h(0)=0 and h(x)=x+exp(-1/x²) for x≠0. The flat exponential extends smoothly with all derivatives zero at 0, so h is C∞ and its Taylor series at 0 is x. Yet h(x)-x is positive for all nonzero x, so h is not analytic there. The Taylor coefficients need not all be zero.
major_error_concepts: The function |x| proves that C∞ functions can fail to be analytic at 0 because |x| is infinitely differentiable there.

cards.prompt: Define Taylor remainder error bound. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The uniform consequence that a bound M on the next derivative yields absolute remainder at most M times the absolute displacement to the power n plus one divided by factorial n plus one.
required_concepts: First material clause: The uniform consequence that a bound M on the next derivative yields absolute remainder at most
Remaining material clause: M times the absolute displacement to the power n plus one divided by factorial n plus one.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a numerical approximation without a valid M.

cards.term: Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder: role
cards.prompt: What is Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It represents a smooth function by a local polynomial plus a derivative-controlled remainder, enabling approximation and error bounds; a formal Taylor series without remainder control need not equal the function.
required_concepts: It represents a smooth function by a local polynomial plus a derivative-controlled remainder, enabling approximation and error bounds
a formal Taylor series without remainder control need not equal the function.
major_error_concepts: Using a derivative bound not known on the interval between a and x.

cards.prompt: State Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder under a sufficient C^(n+1) interval hypothesis.
cards.definition: If f is C^(n+1) on an interval containing a and x, then f(x)=sum_{k=0}^n f^(k)(a)(x-a)^k/k! + f^(n+1)(xi)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)! for some xi between a and x (the a=x case is immediate). The intermediate point may depend on x. The remainder term, not formal infinite-series notation alone, controls the approximation error.
required_concepts: State a sufficient C^(n+1) interval hypothesis.
Give the Taylor polynomial plus the (n+1)st-derivative Lagrange remainder.
xi lies between the expansion and evaluation points and may depend on x.
major_error_concepts: Continuity of f alone guarantees every degree-n Taylor formula, with the same xi for all x.

cards.prompt: What is Two-function cross-multiplied mean-value theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It compares increments of two functions through their derivatives and underlies Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem and rigorous l'Hopital-style arguments; denominator derivative and nondegeneracy conditions cannot be ignored.
required_concepts: It compares increments of two functions through their derivatives and underlies Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem and rigorous l'Hopital-style arguments
denominator derivative and nondegeneracy conditions cannot be ignored.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by the second derivative without proving it nonzero.

cards.prompt: State Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem in cross-multiplied form, and identify what is needed before dividing.
cards.definition: If real functions f and g are continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with a<b, then some c in (a,b) satisfies [f(b)-f(a)]g'(c)=[g(b)-g(a)]f'(c). This cross-multiplied form requires no division and no nonzero derivative assumption. A quotient version additionally requires the relevant denominator quantities to be nonzero.
required_concepts: Both functions are continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on its interior.
State the cross-multiplied equality at one common interior c.
Nonzero denominator conditions are added only if dividing.
major_error_concepts: The cross-multiplied theorem guarantees [f(b)-f(a)]/[g(b)-g(a)]=f'(c)/g'(c) even when g is constant.

cards.prompt: Define Accumulation function continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] and |f(t)|≤M there, then F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt is M-Lipschitz: |F(y)-F(x)|≤M|y-x| for all x,y in [a,b]. Hence F is continuous even when f has discontinuities. Boundedness without Riemann integrability is not enough to define this F in the Riemann sense.
required_concepts: f is Riemann integrable on the interval.
A bound |f|≤M yields |F(y)-F(x)|≤M|y-x|.
Continuity of F does not assert differentiability at every point.
major_error_concepts: Every bounded function, including the rational-indicator Dirichlet function, defines a Riemann accumulation integral on a nondegenerate interval.

cards.prompt: What is Accumulation-integral differentiation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It shows that accumulating a continuous integrand creates an antiderivative and recovers the integrand by differentiation, linking local rates to area; weaker regularity changes the pointwise conclusion.
required_concepts: It shows that accumulating a continuous integrand creates an antiderivative and recovers the integrand by differentiation, linking local rates to area
weaker regularity changes the pointwise conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Replacing pointwise continuity with mere integrability or quoting antiderivative notation as proof.

cards.prompt: State the pointwise FTC for an accumulation integral, separating the integrability and continuity assumptions.
cards.definition: Let f be Riemann integrable on [a,b] and continuous at c in (a,b). Then F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt is differentiable at c and F'(c)=f(c). Integrability makes F defined, while continuity at c establishes this pointwise derivative. Mere integrability alone does not guarantee the equality at every point.
required_concepts: Require Riemann integrability on the interval.
Require continuity of f at the interior point c.
The accumulation derivative at c equals f(c).
major_error_concepts: Because f is Riemann integrable, F'(c)=f(c) must hold at every discontinuity as well.

cards.prompt: Define Additivity over adjacent intervals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that integrability and integral split at an interior point with partitions reconciled across both subintervals.
required_concepts: The theorem that integrability and integral split at an interior point with partitions reconciled across both subintervals.
major_error_concepts: Double-counting or omitting the split point as a width contribution.

cards.prompt: Define Algebra and order of integrals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The linearity monotonicity absolute-value and product integrability properties with boundedness and proof dependencies explicit.
required_concepts: The linearity monotonicity absolute-value and product integrability properties with boundedness and proof dependencies explicit.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion before proving the absolute-value function integrable.

cards.term: Change of variables for Riemann integrals
cards.prompt: State a continuous-integrand change-of-variables theorem for Riemann integrals, retaining orientation.
cards.definition: If phi is C¹ on [a,b] and f is continuous on an interval containing phi([a,b]), then integral_a^b f(phi(t))phi'(t)dt = integral_{phi(a)}^{phi(b)} f(u)du. The derivative factor and oriented bounds are essential. In this continuous-integrand version phi need not be one-to-one or monotone; weaker Riemann-integrability variants require their own hypotheses.
required_concepts: Use a C¹ change phi and continuous f on its image interval.
Transform both the differential factor and the oriented bounds.
Do not impose monotonicity as universally necessary for this version.
major_error_concepts: Substitution removes phi'(t), and the new integral must always run from the smaller transformed endpoint to the larger one without a sign.

cards.prompt: Define Continuous-function integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable via uniform continuity.
required_concepts: The theorem that every continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable via uniform continuity.
major_error_concepts: Using pointwise continuity with one undeclared global delta.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous-integrand average-value theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It realizes the average value of a continuous integrand as an attained function value and supports weighted or physical mean interpretations; continuity and a nondegenerate interval matter, and the realizing point need not be unique.
required_concepts: It realizes the average value of a continuous integrand as an attained function value and supports weighted or physical mean interpretations
continuity and a nondegenerate interval matter, and the realizing point need not be unique.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion for an arbitrary integrable discontinuous function or confusing it with a derivative mean-value theorem.

cards.prompt: State Continuous-integrand average-value theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The proof that a continuous real integrand on a compact interval attains the value of its integral divided by interval length using extremum bounds and connected image.
required_concepts: The proof that a continuous real integrand on a compact interval attains the value of its integral divided by interval length using extremum bounds
and connected image.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion for an arbitrary integrable discontinuous function or confusing it with a derivative mean-value theorem.

cards.prompt: Define Darboux integrability criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The equality of upper and lower integrals equivalently for every epsilon a partition with upper-minus-lower sum below epsilon.
required_concepts: The equality of upper and lower integrals equivalently for every epsilon a partition with upper-minus-lower sum below epsilon.
major_error_concepts: Checking one small numerical gap for a fixed epsilon.

cards.prompt: Define Dirichlet nonintegrability example. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The everywhere-discontinuous rational-indicator function whose every subinterval has infimum zero and supremum one.
required_concepts: The everywhere-discontinuous rational-indicator function whose every subinterval has infimum zero and supremum one.
major_error_concepts: Choosing sample points to make a favorable Riemann sum.

cards.prompt: Define Finite Riemann partition and mesh. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite ordered subdivision of one compact interval with subinterval convention and maximum subinterval length declared for Darboux and Riemann arguments.
required_concepts: A finite ordered subdivision of one compact interval with subinterval convention and maximum subinterval length declared for Darboux and Riemann arguments.
major_error_concepts: Treating an infinite grid or unordered sample as a Riemann partition.

cards.prompt: Define Improper-integral boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The definition of an unbounded-interval or singular-endpoint integral as a limit of proper integrals with convergence proved separately.
required_concepts: The definition of an unbounded-interval or singular-endpoint integral as a limit of proper integrals with convergence proved separately.
major_error_concepts: Treating the infinity symbol as an endpoint in a Riemann partition.

cards.prompt: What is Integration by parts theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers a derivative between factors in an integral and is the integral counterpart of the product rule, supporting estimates and transform identities; boundary terms and regularity assumptions must be retained.
required_concepts: It transfers a derivative between factors in an integral and is the integral counterpart of the product rule, supporting estimates and transform identities
boundary terms and regularity assumptions must be retained.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula when required derivatives are not integrable.

cards.prompt: State definite integration by parts under sufficient regularity hypotheses.
cards.definition: If u,v are C¹ on [a,b], then integral_a^b u(t)v'(t)dt = u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-integral_a^b u'(t)v(t)dt. Both integrals exist under these hypotheses. More general valid versions are acceptable if their regularity and integrability assumptions are stated.
required_concepts: State the boundary product evaluated at b minus a.
The remaining integral has a minus sign and moves the derivative from v to u.
Give C¹ functions as a sufficient hypothesis or a correct qualified weaker version.
major_error_concepts: Integration by parts gives integral u v'=uv+integral u'v with no boundary evaluation.

cards.prompt: Define Monotone-function integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every bounded monotone function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable by telescoping oscillation control.
required_concepts: The theorem that every bounded monotone function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable by telescoping oscillation control.
major_error_concepts: Assuming monotone functions are continuous.

cards.prompt: Define Oscillation criterion for Riemann integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The characterization that a bounded function is integrable when high-oscillation sets can be covered with sufficiently small total interval length at first-course depth.
required_concepts: First material clause: The characterization that a bounded function is integrable when high-oscillation sets
Remaining material clause: can be covered with sufficiently small total interval length at first-course depth.
major_error_concepts: Invoking measure-zero language without constructing the required covers.

cards.prompt: What is Riemann antiderivative evaluation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It evaluates a definite integral from any antiderivative and completes the bridge between differentiation and integration; existence of an antiderivative under the theorem's hypotheses must not be assumed for arbitrary functions.
required_concepts: It evaluates a definite integral from any antiderivative and completes the bridge between differentiation and integration
existence of an antiderivative under the theorem's hypotheses must not be assumed for arbitrary functions.
major_error_concepts: Using an arbitrary antiderivative when its derivative is not known Riemann integrable.

cards.prompt: State the Riemann antiderivative evaluation theorem, including the derivative-integrability requirement.
cards.definition: Suppose F is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and its derivative has a Riemann-integrable extension f to [a,b]. Then integral_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a). Endpoint values assigned to f do not affect the integral. An arbitrary derivative need not be Riemann integrable, so the integrability premise is substantive.
required_concepts: F is continuous through the endpoints and differentiable in the interior.
Its derivative is Riemann integrable after harmless endpoint assignment.
The integral equals F(b)-F(a).
major_error_concepts: Every derivative is automatically Riemann integrable, so an antiderivative symbol alone proves the evaluation formula.

cards.prompt: Define Step and piecewise-continuous integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The integrability of functions with finitely many jumps or finitely many continuous pieces after isolating discontinuities.
required_concepts: The integrability of functions with finitely many jumps or finitely many continuous pieces after isolating discontinuities.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every function with infinitely many discontinuities is nonintegrable.

cards.prompt: Define Upper and lower Darboux integrals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The infimum of upper sums and supremum of lower sums with lower integral never exceeding upper integral.
required_concepts: The infimum of upper sums and supremum of lower sums with lower integral never exceeding upper integral.
major_error_concepts: Taking the infimum and supremum in the wrong directions.

cards.prompt: Define Upper and lower Darboux sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sums of subinterval suprema or infima times widths for a bounded function with their order under refinement.
required_concepts: The sums of subinterval suprema or infima times widths for a bounded function with their order under refinement.
major_error_concepts: Assuming upper and lower sums use sampled values.

cards.term: Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth: role
cards.prompt: What is Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns uniform boundedness or pointwise precompactness plus equicontinuity into a uniformly convergent subsequence, providing compactness for families of functions; pointwise boundedness without equicontinuity is insufficient.
required_concepts: It turns uniform boundedness or pointwise precompactness plus equicontinuity into a uniformly convergent subsequence, providing compactness for families of functions
pointwise boundedness without equicontinuity is insufficient.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform boundedness alone gives compactness.

cards.term: Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth
cards.prompt: State Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The compactness criterion that an equicontinuous pointwise relatively compact or uniformly bounded real-valued family on a compact metric domain has uniformly convergent subsequences.
required_concepts: First material clause: The compactness criterion that an equicontinuous pointwise relatively compact or uniformly
Remaining material clause: bounded real-valued family on a compact metric domain has uniformly convergent subsequences.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform boundedness alone gives compactness.

cards.prompt: Define Completeness of bounded-function sup norm. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that bounded functions into a complete scalar field form a complete normed space under the supremum norm.
required_concepts: The theorem that bounded functions into a complete scalar field form a complete normed space under the supremum norm.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every function subspace is closed and complete.

cards.prompt: What is Derivative-limit interchange theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It supplies conditions under which a limit of differentiable functions remains differentiable with derivative equal to the derivative limit; pointwise convergence of functions and derivatives alone is generally too weak.
required_concepts: It supplies conditions under which a limit of differentiable functions remains differentiable with derivative equal to the derivative limit
pointwise convergence of functions and derivatives alone is generally too weak.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform convergence of f_n alone preserves derivatives.

cards.prompt: State a sufficient compact-interval theorem for interchanging differentiation and a sequence limit.
cards.definition: A sufficient version is: f_n are C¹ on a fixed compact interval [a,b], f_n(x_0) converges at some x_0 in [a,b], and f_n' converges uniformly there to g. Then f_n converges uniformly to a C¹ function f and f'=g on the interval interior, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. On a disconnected domain, one anchor point does not control arbitrary constants on other components.
required_concepts: Use a fixed compact interval and C¹ functions as sufficient regularity.
Derivative convergence is uniform and function values converge at one anchor.
The functions converge uniformly to a differentiable limit whose derivative is g.
major_error_concepts: Uniform convergence of derivatives on two disjoint intervals plus one anchor on the first controls additive constants on the second.

cards.prompt: Give a uniformly convergent sequence of differentiable functions for which derivative convergence fails, and verify the failure.
cards.definition: Take f_n(x)=sin(nx)/n on R. Since |f_n(x)|≤1/n for every x, f_n→0 uniformly. But f_n'(x)=cos(nx), and at x=pi these derivatives alternate between -1 and 1 rather than converge to the derivative 0 of the limit. Thus even uniform function convergence does not by itself justify derivative convergence.
required_concepts: Give an explicit sequence of differentiable functions.
Verify uniform convergence of the functions to their stated limit.
Show at a specified point that their derivatives do not converge to the derivative of the limit; the reference sine sequence is only one valid witness.
accepted_variants: Another example is f_n(x)=sin(n²x)/n on R. The bound |f_n|≤1/n proves uniform convergence to 0, but f_n'(0)=n diverges rather than approaching the derivative 0 of the limit.
major_error_concepts: The uniform bound on sin(nx)/n forces cos(nx) to converge to zero at every x.

cards.prompt: What is Dini theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It upgrades monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to uniform convergence on a compact space when the limit is continuous; each compactness, monotonicity, and continuity condition carries real force.
required_concepts: It upgrades monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to uniform convergence on a compact space when the limit is continuous
each compactness, monotonicity, and continuity condition carries real force.
major_error_concepts: Dropping compactness continuity or monotonicity.

cards.prompt: State Dini theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The compact-domain result that monotone pointwise convergence of continuous real functions to a continuous limit is uniform.
required_concepts: The compact-domain result that monotone pointwise convergence of continuous real functions to a continuous limit is uniform.
major_error_concepts: Dropping compactness continuity or monotonicity.

cards.prompt: What claim does Discontinuous pointwise-limit counterexample refute, and why?
cards.definition: On [0,1], let f_n(x)=x^n. Each f_n is continuous. The pointwise limit is 0 for 0≤x<1 and 1 at x=1, so it is discontinuous at 1. The convergence is not uniform: the supremum error remains 1, although it is approached rather than attained on x<1. This does not contradict preservation of continuity by uniform limits.
required_concepts: Give continuous functions on a common domain and identify their pointwise limit.
Exhibit and justify a discontinuity of that limit.
Explain why this does not contradict continuity preservation under uniform convergence; the x^n witness is illustrative, not mandatory.
accepted_variants: On [0,1], f_n(x)=min(1,nx) is continuous and converges pointwise to f(0)=0 and f(x)=1 for x>0. The limit is discontinuous at 0, so convergence cannot be uniform. This is a different valid witness from x^n.
major_error_concepts: x^n converges uniformly on [0,1] to a discontinuous function, disproving continuity preservation by uniform convergence.

cards.prompt: Define Equicontinuity of a function family. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The common local modulus property controlling all family members at once with uniform equicontinuity distinguished.
required_concepts: The common local modulus property controlling all family members at once with uniform equicontinuity distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Confusing bounded function values with equicontinuity.

cards.prompt: Define Limit-operation dependency matrix. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The explicit mapping from each desired continuity integral derivative sum or power-series interchange to its sufficient hypotheses counterexamples and proof dependency.
required_concepts: First material clause: The explicit mapping from each desired continuity integral derivative sum or power-series
Remaining material clause: interchange to its sufficient hypotheses counterexamples and proof dependency.
major_error_concepts: Using interchange by visual symmetry of notation.

cards.prompt: Define pointwise convergence, and explain whether a uniform convergence proof also establishes it.
